title: A Natural Gas Project Off Alaska’s Coast May Be a Russian Ploy for Intel on the Arctic
author: Heather Vogell
content:
To an outsider, the research boats bobbing in the frigid and stormy Beaufort
Sea off Alaska would seem little cause for alarm. Oil and gas companies have
regularly explored the area for decades.

For this project, businessmen from the United Arab Emirates were touting a
plan to tap the vast natural gas reserves that lay beneath the tundra of
Alaska’s North Slope. They promised the operation would eventually be
American-owned. No one could dispute Alaska’s dire energy needs — not to
mention the potential for lucrative exports.

The surveyors last year used specialized equipment to map the depth and shape
of the seabed, collect samples of shallow marine sediments and conduct sonar
scans to check for obstructions such as shipwrecks. Documents show that their
work was not far, as the crow flies, from the start of the Trans-Alaska
Pipeline System — a cornerstone of U.S. energy production. An Air Force long-
range radar station sat just to the west. More than 100 miles off the coast,
the Navy’s fast-attack nuclear submarines sometimes practiced surfacing
through the thick Arctic ice.

But this project was far from routine. While the contractors performing the
work were American, the UAE company paying for the surveys was actually being
steered by Russia’s liquefied natural gas giant, Novatek — a company under
partial U.S. sanctions, documents and interviews show.

The proposal to create an LNG processing plant on Alaska’s coast has already
put reams of scientific data about the strategically critical region within
reach of Novatek’s leader, an oligarch who is close to President Vladimir
Putin, a ProPublica investigation found.

The Financial Times and The New York Times [reported on the Russian ties to
the venture ](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/in-us-gas-talks-
with-kremlin-hidden-financing-for-alaska-project-emerges.html)last month. But
the extent to which the company gathered detailed information about sensitive
areas of Alaska has not been previously disclosed.

Such information is highly valuable in the ever-changing and unpredictable
Arctic, with its potential routes for both naval ships and missiles.
[Norwegian security services](https://www.reuters.com/world/norways-security-
service-sees-stepped-up-russian-espionage-arctic-2026-02-06/) and [U.S.
lawmakers](https://www.lee.senate.gov/2026/6/lee-shaheen-introduce-bipartisan-
bill-keeping-foreign-spies-out-of-american-waters) have expressed concerns
this year about the danger of increased spy and sabotage operations by Russia
in the Arctic.

Russia-backed information gathering so close to the U.S. shoreline can be seen
as “a direct challenge to sovereignty and security,” said Heather Conley, a
former State Department official who is now a senior fellow with the American
Enterprise Institute.

“It's super, super sensitive,” she said, adding, “Any scientific data, it
immediately is dual use,” meaning it can serve both military and civilian
ends.

Information on changing sea ice and other conditions off the North Slope could
help Russia plan activities that undermine U.S. security, said Troy Bouffard,
director of the Center for Arctic Security and Resilience at the University of
Alaska, Fairbanks. The fact that the surveys were given permits and done
without interference could be seen as an intelligence failure, he said.

Bouffard added that it’s “highly unlikely” that intelligence personnel didn’t
learn of the effort because any work in the austere, remote and militarily
sensitive North Slope area stands out.

“All this is really surprising,” Bouffard said. “Should not have happened.”

The surveys were conducted in the second half of 2025, paused during harsh
weather, then restarted in mid-2026, documents and sources say. By late August
2026, dozens of contractors were stationed on three large vessels — the Annika
Marie, the Ukpik and the Uŋalaq — loaded with equipment for tasks such as
monitoring waves, testing currents, and tides, and drilling core samples in
the mud, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Then, in September, the CEO of the project’s U.S. arm, Polar Train LNG,
resigned, questioned the operation’s legality and asserted it was a Russian
ploy to gain control of a strategic U.S. asset, Alaska’s [natural gas
reserves](https://www.doi.gov/pressreleases/usgs-releases-assessment-
undiscovered-natural-gas-resources-alaskas-north-slope).

In 2025, the survey work was focused on an area just west of Prudhoe Bay,
which is near where the pipeline originates, documents and sources say. The
next year, as the area thawed, Polar Train’s CEO, Joel Riddle, and his team
told his financiers that location was not ideal for an LNG operation because
of the high cost of dredging that would be needed and the potential to
interfere with whaling by local residents. They urged the company’s UAE parent
to focus on a site more than 250 miles to the west.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261109-alaska-afk-
coast-map-grey.jpg?w=752)A page from a Tech Wave presentation on plans to
locate a liquified natural gas operation in Alaska. Polar Train LNG is a
subsidiary of UAE-based Tech Wave. Reviewed by ProPublica

But the UAE company asserted its control over the purportedly American outfit
Riddle led in late August and ordered the contractors offshore to head back to
a site closer to Prudhoe Bay. Riddle resigned the next month, on Sept. 19,
warning that Polar Train’s “investments” were “very likely sooner or later to
trigger” a federal inquiry.

Polar Train had applied to the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets
Control the month before, seeking a waiver of U.S. sanctions to allow it to
purchase a partially built LNG plant sitting in a Murmansk, Russia, shipyard
and transport it to Alaska.

“Deploying this technology in Alaska serves not only to unlock U.S. LNG
resources in the Pacific basin closer to key export markets in Asia,” said the
application, which ProPublica obtained, “but also to ensure this cutting-edge
equipment is deployed primarily to the benefit of the United States rather
than Russia.”

The six-page application did not make clear who was behind the effort,
steering the financing and decision-making needed to get the venture off the
ground. The document’s digital properties held a clue: Many computer
applications include what is known as metadata in a document that can reveal
who has previously worked on it. In this instance, the OFAC application was
signed by a lawyer in Washington, D.C., but the author’s name was listed in
the metadata in Cyrillic: Evgeniya Kononova, a lawyer whose LinkedIn profile
says she is deputy head of legal for Novatek in Moscow.

[Novatek said in a
statement](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28878731-novateks-
response/#document/p1) to ProPublica that it “provided technical and other
information” about its equipment for the waiver request, providing “comments
to the draft application.” The company did not answer a list of specific
questions, including inquiries about Kononova’s role.

It’s not clear whether the Russian natural gas executives backing the project
hope to operate an LNG plant in Alaska or have a more immediate goal in mind —
like finishing the incomplete plant that sanctions had stranded in Russia or
gathering intelligence for the Kremlin in a strategically important region.

In a statement to ProPublica, Novatek denied it is gathering intelligence
through the project, saying: “We state clearly and categorically: any such
claims or implications are false.”

Novatek said it is “focused on utilizing its technology in Alaska and views
this opportunity as a standalone and self-sufficient project.” The company
said decisions about the project’s surveys “and other operational matters”
were made by Polar Train and its UAE parent, Tech Wave Industrial Project
Management.

The revelations about the Alaska LNG project come as the Trump administration
has scaled back [rules requiring U.S.
companies](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0603) to report
their true owners, cut back [counterintelligence squads in the
FBI](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/g-s1-145511/fbi-trump-counterintelligence-
units-cuts) and disbanded a Department of Justice task force aimed at seizing
[Russian oligarchs’ assets](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-
administration-ends-biden-era-task-force-aimed-at-seizing-russian-oligarchs-
assets).

Reduced staffing makes counterintelligence more difficult, said Emily Harding,
a former CIA analyst and former deputy director of the Senate intelligence
committee under Republicans.

“It’s not just that you need people knowledgeable about the
counterintelligence mission, but you need people knowledgeable about highly
technical topical areas,” she said. “That’s a big problem in normal times, but
especially hard when staffing is down.”

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment last week.

ProPublica’s account of the Polar Train LNG project is drawn from interviews
with a dozen people and documents that include corporate records,
correspondence, and memos, as well as presentations detailing the survey work,
budgets, a wire transfer receipt, and loan agreements.

On Saturday, Polar Train LNG said its research in Alaska “involved a standard
set of surveys routinely conducted by companies worldwide.” The data collected
is not classified, it said, and “all activities complied with applicable
laws.” The purpose of the work was to find an appropriate site for the LNG
project, the company said.

The White House has sought to leverage energy deals involving Russia as an
incentive to negotiate an end to the war with Ukraine. Putin has spoken
publicly about his desire to cooperate with the U.S. in the Arctic,
potentially through Novatek.

“We are discussing with our American partners the possibility of working
together in this field, not only in our Arctic zone but also in Alaska,” he
[said in August 2025](https://tass.com/economy/2006431), days after meeting
with Trump at a summit in Anchorage.

In September, Putin talked about Polar Train LNG’s project with President
Donald Trump’s peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, The New York
Times reported last month. Polar Train’s U.S. parent has also filed an
application with the Treasury Department in hopes of importing LNG to Alaska
directly from Russia, according to a person familiar with the request.

When he resigned as CEO, Riddle accused Novatek of “financing and ultimately
controlling the strategic direction” of the supposedly American-led Polar
Train.

[Polar Train, now under new leadership, denied
that](https://polarlng.com/polar-lng-fact-sheet/) Novatek is “secretly
financing” the project, in a statement it posted on its website.

All three companies said Novatek had agreed to buy a minority stake in the
Alaska operation and had paid Tech Wave an undisclosed amount of money. The
deal, they said, is contingent on Tech Wave attracting American investment
totaling more than 50%. Novatek simultaneously said it “did not provide any
funding to the Project.”

”We would like to note, however, that provision of debt financing, including
to U.S. persons, is not prohibited.” Novatek did not answer questions from
ProPublica about whether it has provided debt financing to the Alaska project.

In its website statement, Polar Train called Riddle “a disgruntled employee”
and said he was “recently terminated from the company for cause.”

“You can’t legally terminate someone who’s already resigned,” Riddle said.
Tech Wave’s termination notice, which accused Riddle of announcing plans to
launch a competing LNG project, was dated six days after his resignation,
copies of both documents show. The notice was signed by a new acting CEO, Tim
Talkington.

In a statement to ProPublica on Saturday, Talkington said that the U.S. has “a
generational opportunity to advance U.S. energy dominance, unlock profound
benefits for the state of Alaska, and strengthen American Arctic navigation.”

### An Audacious Plan

![A 3D CAD engineering model rendering of an industrial
facility.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261109-alaska-afk-schematic-structure.jpg?w=752)A
schematic drawing of the liquified natural gas processing facility Polar Train
LNG is asking to bring to Alaska Polar Train OFAC waiver application

The audacious LNG project was launched in 2025, when a half dozen executives
with ExxonMobil sat down with representatives of Abu Dhabi-based Tech Wave
Industrial Project Management, which was eyeing Alaska for an LNG facility,
according to a person familiar with the project.

Tech Wave was 95% owned by Norwegian [Bjorn
Gundersen](https://www.thebarentsobserver.com/industry-and-energy/big-brag-
about-novateks-grand-arctic-projects-but-zero-comments-for-the-press/137912).
He’d served as a deputy director for Novatek and played a key role in
developing one of the most technologically ambitious LNG projects ever, known
as Arctic LNG 2, on the Gydan Peninsula in Russia’s Far North. Gundersen and
Tech Wave’s CEO, Rajeev Lehar, assured Exxon and others that no Russian money
was involved in their project, the person said.

Tech Wave said in a statement Saturday that “Novatek offers the only proven
technology suited to Arctic conditions” that also meets the project’s
timeline. The company’s expertise is “informed in part” by Gundersen’s
experience working on Arctic LNG 2, the company said.

Reached in Abu Dhabi on Saturday, Gundersen declined to comment. Exxonmobil
did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech Wave’s plan was to seek permission to buy state-of-the-art natural gas
equipment from Novatek that was meant for Arctic LNG 2 before U.S. economic
sanctions prevented the company from finishing the work. The incomplete
apparatus, built atop a concrete platform that is the size of nearly 10
football fields, was sitting in a Russian shipyard. Tech Wave wanted to bring
the equipment by sea to Alaska’s North Slope, where it could begin processing
and selling millions of metric tons of liquified natural gas that had been
trapped in the ground for decades. The project would need to reach an
agreement with the oil and gas companies already working in the area, since
the natural gas it wanted was a byproduct of their extraction work.

Tech Wave had been exploring possible sites for the plant in the summer of
2025, before its leaders met with the Exxon executives, according to documents
obtained by ProPublica and interviews.

It also dispatched the first group of surveyors who worked off the coast near
Prudhoe Bay, collecting detailed information about the seabed.

Riddle was hired in March 2026 as Polar Train LNG’s CEO. Documents show his
employment agreement was signed by Gentry Beach, [a Texas
investor](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-jr-toes-fuzzy-line-as-
undisclosed-partner-gets-access/) who was a college friend of Donald Trump Jr.
and helped raise money for President Trump’s campaign in 2016. Beach, who took
part in meetings about the Alaska project, later told The Financial Times that
he had an “incredible relationship” with oligarch Leonid Mikhelson, the
Novatek founder and CEO.

Beach did not respond to requests for comment. Novatek said “Gentry Beach has
no connection” with the company.

Riddle previously led the Australian fracking operation Tamboran Resources,
where he developed a business relationship with Chris Wright, who was
confirmed as Trump’s energy secretary in February 2025. Wright had been CEO of
the fracking giant Liberty Energy, which partnered with Tamboran in 2023.

![A man with gray hair pointing upward.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261108-alaska-lng-mikhelson.jpg?w=752)Leonid
Mikhelson, the founder and chief of Russia’s largest private gas group,
Novatek, on July 20, 2023 Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images

It wasn’t long before the actions of the UAE leaders made Riddle suspicious
about who was behind the company and what their motives were.

Early on, Riddle said he and his team sought information on how Tech Wave
spent tens of millions of dollars before he came on the project, including
doing the surveys. “They were very hesitant to provide details around the cost
or origin of the money that supported the company before I was hired,” Riddle
said.

Riddle said Gundersen wanted to locate the LNG plant just off the coast near
Prudhoe Bay, an area that includes the largest oil field in North America, the
start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and operations by companies that include
Exxon, ConocoPhillips and Hilcorp. The site is near, too, to the [Oliktok Long
Range Radar Site](https://www.jber.jb.mil/News/Photos/igphoto/2000053814/).
Such installations watch for inbound missiles and aircraft and play a critical
role in national defense because satellites don’t have good visibility over
the poles. Prudhoe Bay is a key location, as well, for communications
infrastructure supporting the military and residents in northern Alaska,
through [a subsea fiber optic cable](https://quintillionglobal.com/why-subsea-
cable-security-is-essential-for-national-security/) that originates there and
stretches to Nome.

Riddle advised Tech Wave to consider a different site, near Wainwright, saying
it would require less dredging and would not interfere with whaling by Alaska
residents. He hired another team of surveyors for about $10 million to scope
out that area, records and interviews show.

At the time, Riddle was becoming concerned that the operation was not truly
the work of Abu Dhabi-based investors, but instead was controlled by Novatek,
and its CEO, Mikhelson, who has close ties to Putin.  

In meetings throughout the summer, Riddle and other Polar Train executives met
with Novatek executives including Mikhelson, according to documents reviewed
by ProPublica and interviews with Riddle. Tech Wave also employed several
others who had worked for Novatek besides Gundersen, according to social media
profiles and documents.

On Aug. 14, Polar Train formally requested permission from the Treasury to
import parts into Russia to complete construction of the LNG processor, and
then to allow Polar Train to buy the plant and bring it to Alaska.

Riddle said his efforts to secure U.S. backing for the project met resistance
from his funders. “For months now, there has been no engagement on
productively achieving substantial US shareholding,” he told Gundersen in a
September letter.

Riddle and his team consulted lawyers on how to handle sanctions issues
related to the project — including concerns from Treasury personnel that
Gundersen “may be acting on behalf” of Novatek. In an Aug. 3 letter, the firm
Baker Botts told Riddle those concerns “could result in heightened regulatory
scrutiny of the Project even absent a direct sanctions prohibition.”

Records show Polar Train’s funding, on paper, came in the form of loans from
Tech Wave and Gundersen.

In late August, however, Riddle asked Gundersen and Lehar for more funding for
Polar Train. In response to his request, he said, an employee connected him
via WhatsApp to Denis Solovyov — a deputy of Mikhelson’s at Novatek. Solovyov
— who has been [lobbying in Brussels and Washington against tougher sanctions
on Russian energy](https://en.highnorthnews.com/business/novatek-executive-
traveling-to-brussels-to-soften-eu-stance-on-russian-lng-sources-say/155128) —
promised Riddle he would send money. Solovyov did not respond to a request for
comment.

Joel Riddle| Denis - in our meeting on Tuesday, you committed to facilitating the new funding by the end of this week. Can you please let me know the status? Thanks. | 9:03am  
---|---|---  
Denis Solovyov| The initial funds are already on their way; for stable
financing, I need an approved budget and a weekly payment schedule.| 10:40 am  
August 21, 2026

Messages show Solovyov and Riddle discussed unpaid bills, payroll, budgets and
loan proceeds sent to Polar Train, which were routed through as many as three
other companies, records show.

Joel Riddle| Denis - I have now received confirmation that all information
requested by Rashid and Catherine has been provided. It is critical that the
new funding agreed is wired on the morning of Aug 27th. If funding is not
received, Polar will not be able to make payroll for its employees and pay
critical bills, which will negatively impact the reputation of the company.|
1:07am  
---|---|---  
Denis Solovyov| Joel, Katerina confirmed to me that the funds should be in
your account on the morning of August 27. We are doing everything we can.|
1:46am  
Joel Riddle| Thanks Denis
![🙏](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f64f.png)| 1:47am  
Denis Solovyov| How did your meeting in Alaska go?| 1:52am  
Joel Riddle| Dinner just finished, Secretary Wright is very supportive. I also
have a 1:1 planned with him tomorrow| 1:54am  
August 27, 2026

In the meantime, Riddle had dispatched boats to survey his preferred project
site near Wainwright. But Tech Wave pushed to move the operation back to
Prudhoe Bay, which it said would be quicker and cheaper. Lehar, Tech Wave’s
CEO, sent Polar Train orders Aug. 20 to tell contractors to “cease and suspend
works and services related to the Wainwright site.”

That day, Tech Wave also asserted its control over Polar Train’s spending,
directing Riddle to follow a budget it provided. The plan allocated $13
million for summer field surveys near Prudhoe Bay that included studies of the
seabed, weather and oceanographic conditions, records show. The UAE company
also barred Riddle from obtaining any financing for Polar Train without Tech
Wave’s approval.

Tensions between the American executives and their backers in UAE and Russia
culminated in a meeting in a lavish private suite at the Four Seasons Hotel in
Abu Dhabi between Riddle and Mikhelson on Aug. 31. Riddle said he tried again
to convince Mikhelson and Tech Wave that Wainwright was the only location that
made sense for the project. Mikhelson told Riddle that a Prudhoe Bay area site
was non-negotiable. Riddle told him he’d consider their position and do what
was in the best interest of the company.

In the days that followed, Riddle again became concerned about making payroll.

“Denis please confirm the new funding that was agreed last Monday will be
transferred no later than Monday 7th,” Riddle wrote on Sept. 6 to Mikhelson’s
deputy. In Solovyov’s next message to Riddle in the chat the following day, he
wrote that “the first 5 million were supposed to arrive by today.”

Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank on Sept. 7 wired $5 million from Tech Wave to a
holding company called Polar Eagle, the U.S. parent company of Polar Train,
records show. A Tech Wave employee messaged Riddle the next day saying that
“PE is making a wire transfer to PT."

Tech Wave’s funding came via a loan from a UAE financial services company,
records say.

In statements, Tech Wave and Polar Train LNG said the company has been “funded
exclusively by Tech Wave, through both personal investments by Mr. Gundersen
and borrowed funds.”

Joel Riddle| Denis - I just had calls with both EDF and State - this was to
introduce the potential Murmansk trip in late Sept. I noticed from both of
these calls there was a material uptick in anti-Russia sentiment. I’ll
continue to push on the trip but wanted to just share this feedback - how
should I respond?| 9:59am  
---|---|---  
Denis Solovyov| Joel, thanks for the information. How is this anti-Russian
sentiment manifesting itself? Positive news should be coming our soon.
Besides, the Graham Act is currently on hold.| 12:39pm  
September 3, 2026

The Graham Act, which was named for the late South Carolina Sen. Lindsay
Graham and expanded the sanctions on Russia, was signed into law Sept. 18.
Riddle resigned the next day, and several others followed.

“They wanted to have Russian technology controlling the resource and the North
Slope,” Riddle said. “I just felt like that was not in the U.S. interest.”

In meetings with energy and state officials, Riddle said he told them what
he’d learned about Novatek’s backing for the project. Energy officials said
they would alert the FBI, Riddle said.

With Riddle gone, Polar Train tapped Talkington, who was formerly CEO of
Goldman Sachs Bank Russia in Moscow and sits on the board of Rusal, one of the
world’s largest aluminum producers. The Russian company was founded by
oligarch Oleg Deripaska, who is under U.S. sanctions.

Lehar said in a statement that the company is “ready to work with the Trump
administration” and the state of Alaska. He said the LNG project will, among
other things, “deliver jobs, tax revenue, and more affordable, reliable energy
for Alaskans.”

The status of Polar Train’s application to the Treasury Department is unclear.
On its website, the company says, “LNG deliveries to the market are expected
in 2030.” A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment on the status of the
sanctions waiver, saying the department does not comment on “specific licenses
or applications, including on the existence or lack of any application.”

### Arctic Spying

Russia is keenly aware of the power of information in the Arctic: In January,
Russian authorities [arrested an Arctic public health and environmental
researcher whom they](https://www.thebarentsobserver.com/news/russian-
researcher-who-contributed-to-arctic-council-reports-is-accused-of-state-
treason/444910) accused of treason, saying his work could help Norwegian
intelligence. ([He has denied the
charges](https://t-invariant.org/2026/02/winter-is-coming-why-has-the-fsb-
reclassified-research-on-the-russian-north-as-working-for-foreign-
intelligence/) through a family member.)

The Trump administration’s stance on Russia is in flux. The president and his
representatives have signaled that they hope to use business deals as a carrot
to bring Putin to the negotiating table and end the war in Ukraine. In
October, Trump [signed a
waiver](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/politics/trump-order-russia-
sanctions.html) exempting Russia from the new sanctions laid out in the Graham
Act.

But other U.S. policymakers have been less sanguine. In June, U.S. Sens. Mike
Lee, a Republican from Utah, and Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat from New
Hampshire, [introduced a bipartisan
bill](https://www.lee.senate.gov/2026/6/lee-shaheen-introduce-bipartisan-bill-
keeping-foreign-spies-out-of-american-waters) aimed at stopping spy ships from
countries like China and Russia from conducting research and espionage
operations in U.S. waters.

“This legislation shuts the door to foreign adversaries attempting to commit
espionage and exercise influence at our doorstep in the Arctic,” Lee said
then, “affirming the sole right of the American people to determine who may
approach their shores, from the Aleutians to the Beaufort Sea.”

The Senate [has not acted](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-
congress/senate-bill/4708/all-actions) on the bill.
